newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany pays tribute to gypsy Holocaust victims.
newsitem.headline: Germany pays tribute to gypsy Holocaust victims.

text.p: German President Roman Herzog on Sunday paid tribute to the often forgotten victims of the Nazis -- the Sinti and Roma gypsy community.

Opening an exhibit on the genocide of gypsies, Herzog said: "Along with our Jewish population, you, the Sinti and Roma community, shared the terrible experience of persecution and genocide during the rule of National Socialism," Herzog said.
"The exhibition, which we are opening today, shows how long-running discrimination ended in persecution and murder."
The exhibit is part of a new cultural centre supported by a grant of 10 million marks from the German government.

"The centre should be a bridge to the present and make visible the many contributions of the Sinti and Roma community to German culture," said Romani Rose, leader of Germany's Sinti and Roma community.
Between 1933 and 1945, half a million gypsies were mudered across Europe, including some 20,000 German gypsies.

Parliament President Rita Suessmuth said the fact it had taken 52 years after the end of the Nazi dictatorship to open the centre, reflected how long it had taken the country to recognise the crimes that had been committed against gypsies.
Herzog rejected the theory that gypsies had only been caught up in the Holocaust by chance. "Hitler himself ordered the deportation of all Sinti and Roma to concentration camps."
He said the genocide of gypsies was pushed through out of the same racist motives and with the same intention of a planned and final annihilation as that of the Jews.

Herzog welcomed concentration camp survivors in particular to the event. "If the victims have a lesson for the present, then its is a warning against indifference, self-satisfaction and narrowness," he said.
But Herzog said Germany had still not shaken off all its prejudices about gypsies. "Today we are still not at our goal."
In February German gypsies complained to the European Commission of Human Rights in Strasbourg about a local court ruling which declared them unfit to sub-let apartments.
A court in the western city of Bochum had ruled that gypsies were in general "not appropriate as sub-tenants of an apartment" because they were "a population group which largely has no fixed abode".
Rose said at the time it was important to have the "scandalous judgment" overturned, saying it was reminiscent of persecution of the gypsies under the Nazis.
